items.title: Show HN: Instantly Convert Markdown to PDF/HTML – No Setup Required
items.text: In November2024, I built MD2FILE ( https://md2file.com ) – a Markdown editor and Markdown to PDF converter (two-in-one). I do a lot of documentation, technical notes, and blog posts, and I wanted a tool that could help me edit Markdown easily and also convert Markdown to friendly formats like HTML or PDF for easy sharing with other people. I searched online and while I was inspired by some of the greatest tools, I noticed most were a bit clunky and limited. Some were good but didn't allow users to try them for free before committing. That inspired me to create MD2FILE, a Markdown Editor & Markdown to PDF converter with these features: •GitHub-style markdown that just works •Live preview while you type (WYSIWYG) •Drop in math equations and charts super easily •Quick PDF/HTML export •Customize how your code looks Some features I’m still working on include: - Cloud sync – Connect to Google Drive, Dropbox, GitHub, and publish straight to Blogger or WordPress. - Team mode – collaborate, merge changes smoothly, add inline comments just like in Google Docs. - Offline writing - Integrated comments like it works in Word or Google Docs. To use the tool, users click on OPEN EDITOR at the top, paste their document in Markdown format, edit, and save (export it as HTML or PDF). We are in public beta phase and still fine-tuning the tool to make it more user-friendly. It's the reason I affed the submit feedback button at the top (visible when someone opens the editor) to let users give suggestions for improvement. It's where I got inspiration for creating additional features mentioned above. I would love your feedback on whether MD2FILE addresses your Markdown editing and conversion pain points.

items.title: Ask HN: Algorithms for inline comments?
items.text: I want to put inline comments on my blog. Like GitHub allows you to do (or BitBucket, Diigo, Medium etc). However, I want the comments to 'stick' to the item (paragraph, sentence, image): if I move it to another place in the document, if I make text amends - even if I merge two paragraphs, the comment should remain visible. OK, the comment may not be relevant any more, but then I can 'archive' them with he previous draft (preserving a full history of comments plus text changes). In my research I've found BitBucket's post [1] about how they built theirs, but it lacks detail. I imagine the technical challenges to be similar to Real-time Collaborative Editing [2] - keep track of text changes and re-apply comments to the right place. So I appeal to the HN Community : Are there sample open source implementations out there? What terminology should I be searching for (finding the language of a new problem domain is challenging)? How would you implement it? Are there papers/web pages you can recommend? I believe Operational Transforms [3] are the way to go, but I have no basis for that. 1. http://blog.bitbucket.org/2012/10/30/building-inline-comments-for-pull-requests-and-commits/ 2. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaborative_real-time_editor 3. http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_transformation

items.title: Ask HN: What blog service to use for software/electronic side-projects?
items.text: Good day fellow HNers, I've been looking at alternatives to increase my online presence a little (in ways other than a StackOverflow and GitHub account). I have a number of small side projects that I'd like to write about (on various topics, but mostly electronic and software). I don't expect daily articles, but the ones that will be posted should be reasonably high quality (some howtos, experimental projects, research projects, etc). It also turns out that there are MUCH more blogging platform options available than I thought, including various technical tradeoffs: - Self hosted vs Free cloud based vs Premium cloud based - Static vs Dynamic engines - Varying degrees of interactiveness - etc For those of you who do similar things, what were the things you considered when you made your choice, and what has turned out to be important, ie: - Is user comments and feedback valuable, or a nice to have? - How important is social media integration for a reasonably niche topic? - Is self hosting more trouble than it's worth? (cost and timewise) - Impact on search engine exposure - .... Is it a viable option to self host (just because I want to play around with it) with links to those articles from a more mainstream blogging site? As always, your feedback is much appreciated!

items.title: Show HN: APIRank.dev – We crawled and ranked public APIs from the internet
items.text: tl;dr we at Escape (YC W23), we scanned 5651+ public APIs on the internet with our in house feedback driven API exploration tech, and ranked them using security, performance, reliability, and design criteria. The results are public on https://apirank.dev . You can request that we index your own API to the list for free and see how it compares to others. Why we did that? During a YC meetup I spoke with a fellow founder that told me how hard it was to pick the right external APIs to use within your own projects. I realized that most of what we build relies on public APIs from external vendors, but there was no benchmark to help developers compare and evaluate public APIs before picking one. So we decided to do it ourselves. Say hi to apirank.dev. Why is ranking public APIs hard? Automating Public API technical assessment is a tough problem. First, we needed to find all the public APIs and their specifications - mostly OpenAPI files. We used several strategies to find those: - Crawl API repositories like apis.guru - Crawl Github for openapi.json and openapi.yaml files - A cool google dork Those strategies enabled us to gather around ~20.000 OpenAPI specs. Then lies the hard part of the problem: We want to dynamically evaluate those APIs' security, performance, and reliability. But APIs take parameters that are tightly coupled to the underlying business logic. A naive automated way would not work: putting random data in parameters would likely not pass the API's validation layer, thus giving us little insight into the real API behavior. Manually creating tests for each API is also not sustainable: it would take years for our 10-people team. We needed to do it in an automated way. Fortunately, our main R&D efforts at Escape aimed to generate legitimate traffic against any API efficently. That's how we developed Feedback-Driven API exploration, a new technique that quickly asses the underlying business logic of an API by analyzing responses and dependencies between reques

items.title: Show HN: Scribe – AI search engine: navigate the web your way, minus the noise
items.text: Hi all I've been working on a new search engine for the Internet, called Scribe ( https://goscri.be ). It's entirely powered by AI, with LLMs and embeddings used to classify, rank, and filter results, and built with the intention to bring more quality and power user features. Some of its features include: - All results are evaluated using trained AI models to detect paywalled, spammy, SEO-heavy content. Results are ranked based on merit only. - Get quick, direct, human-friendly answers for questions by an AI assistant, instead of digging through long-form blog posts and documentation. - For longer, deeper discussions, continue searches by chatting with the assistant with saved and searchable conversations. - Quickly preview a page without leaving the search, to quickly evaluate or use the content. Discover related pages from across the whole web, including from unseen corners. - Personalise your results by filtering out sites you don't want to see results from. - Surface quick facts and answers from official and trusted sources without needing to dig into the page. I'm also currently working on: - Leave a comment and rating for a page, share and discuss with friends and family, and collectively filter or label the quality of a page or site right within the results page. - Navigate an entire site using natural language. For example, "cancel an order" on Amazon.com takes you to the cancellation page, "coffee grounds" surfaces those products within a small online shop, etc. - Within a page, quickly jump to a section using natural language, or chat with an AI assistant about the content. - Show videos from the web in the search results. For example, "max s3 buckets" highlights the exact utterance in a talk by AWS that mentions the answer. - A companion that helps you organise, track, jump between, and take notes of what you visit while deep diving, instead of having hundreds of tabs open. items.title: Show HN: I built a Chrome extension pornblocker,it featured on Google webstore
items.text: I wanted to share the rollercoaster ride of creating and launching my Chrome extension, "PornBlocker," which is now proudly featured on the Google Web Store. This journey had everything: a dream, unexpected roadblocks, dramatic turns, and an eventual sweet victory. The story begins about two years ago. I was a recent CS grad with a burning passion to make a difference. The internet, as we all know, can be a wild place, especially for younger audiences and individuals trying to avoid specific types of content. That’s where my idea for PornBlocker began. The goal? To develop an extension that could automatically block adult content, ensuring a safer browsing experience. Initially, I thought the biggest hurdle would be the technical side—building the extension. Little did I know, the real challenge would lie elsewhere. I dove headfirst into coding, spending countless nights converting coffee into code. After three months of rigorous testing and tweaking, PornBlocker was ready. Or so I thought. I excitedly launched it on the Google Web Store, expecting immediate attention and downloads. That’s when I hit my first major roadblock. The extension was there, but it was practically invisible. No downloads, no reviews—nothing. I was devastated. Had I missed something crucial? Was my effort all for naught? Determined to find out why, I started reaching out to users on forums and social media. The feedback was eye-opening but hard to swallow. Users liked the idea but found the extension clunky and the user interface unintuitive. It was back to the drawing board. Over the next few months, I revamped everything from the UI/UX to the underlying algorithms. The second version was sleeker, faster, and more user-friendly. With bated breath, I re-launched it. This time, the response was slightly better. People started downloading it, and some positive reviews trickled in. But then, another turn. items.title: Ask HN: Best way to migrate from Wordpress to something simpler/more elegant?
items.text: I've been running my personal blog [0] on a selfhosted linux box (Hetzner server) for about six years. A lot less experienced back then, I opted for WP. But it is a hassle. I've tried making my site as lightweight as possible, but there's a lot of functionality I just don't need. I'm the sole author/user of my low traffic site. On the technical side - a large attack surface, constant security issues, themes randomly screwing up site access, lots of custom nginx rules to mitigate potential issues and make PHP play along nicely. Content wise - the online editor is a HUGE pain. Probably the biggest reason preventing me from posting more. Also, I tried disabling the inclusion of external resources in the past, but a few days ago I noticed ublock blocking fonts.googleapis.com through my site. I don't want any of this. In short, I'd like to move my content to a new site, preferably something minimalistic, maybe static, with a small footprint and entirely self-contained. No more wonky WYSIWYG editing, constant security worries, MySQL/PHP dependencies. Some thoughts regarding migrating: * Should I keep a list of deeplinks to my posts to integrate as nginx redirects so search engine hits still work? * Are comments overrated? I've had just a few over the years, with mostly mixed relevance. * Depending on the technology used, does it make sense to leverage CI/CD? I'm already running a private gitlab instance for various tasks. I've seen really beautiful personal pages linked on HN in the past. Are there recommendations or positive experiences with selfhosted sites? [0] https://jschumacher.info/

items.title: Beyond Google: the future of shopping and search with ChatGPT
items.text: I've been an indie tech blogger for several years, and the gradually declining page views and organic traffic point toward only one thing: The reach and omniscience of Google Search are on the decline as more people become addicted to ChatGPT. If you keep an ear out on blogging and SEO subs, you'll hear the same thing. When I interact with ChatGPT today, stepping out of my programming shoes and evaluating it as a layperson, I see that the potential here is enormous and very much within the realms of technical feasibility. Many Android apps could vanish from our phones if a few key players, like OpenAI, decide to take the initiative. Imagine a chat with an LLM called BBGPT that's linked to BigBasket: *Me:* Hey BB, please create an order for 1 kg of sugar, 4 packets of Nandini Blue Milk, and 800 grams of Parle-G biscuits. *BB:* Sugar from the Popular or Royal brand? *Me:* Which one tastes better and is healthier? *BB:* They're usually the same for most practical purposes, but you can check the nutrition facts here, if you're interested. *Me:* All right, please confirm the order! *BB:* I've just sent a Google Pay request for UPI payment. *Me:* (Makes the payment). *BB:* Your order is confirmed! Let me know if I can do anything else for you today. *Me:* Thanks BB, you're a great buddy! This is 10x more efficient than placing an order on BigBasket app or website, or any online order for that matter! It's only a matter of time before someone figures this out and starts rolling these changes out. About a decade ago, in 2014, if I had told you that something similar to Tom Riddle's Diary would give a tough competition to the greatest search engine on the planet, you'd probably have laughed at me! But not today, with the advent of ChatGPT. The future is here. The technology is ready. It's only a matter of who, when, and how someone will take the initiative! What do you think about this? Please let me know in the comments.
